quote: Cover@τ , which measures the fraction of problems that a model can solve for which at least a τ proportion of completions are correct.
supports: The paper defines Cover@τ as the fraction of problems on which at least a τ share of sampled completions is correct.

quote: Unlike Pass@k, Cover@τ captures reasoning under an explicit reliability threshold: models that rely on random guessing degrade rapidly as τ increases.
supports: The paper says Cover@τ handles guessing by a reliability threshold: rarely-correct (guess-driven) problems drop out as τ rises.

quote: Pass@k at large k reflects the increasingly higher chance of success in the limit of the number of trials rather than genuine reasoning
supports: The paper argues that on discrete-answer maths tasks large-k Pass@k mostly reflects the chance of success over many trials, not reasoning.

quote: we demonstrate that Pass@k is a weighted average of Cover@τ , with weights from a Beta(1,k) distribution
supports: The paper proves Pass@k equals a Beta(1,k)-weighted average of the Cover@τ curve.

quote: Thus Pass@k primarily captures whether tasks have any nonzero success probability, rather than how reliably they can be solved.
supports: The paper states that at large k Pass@k only records whether a problem has nonzero success probability.

quote: model achieves Pass@k = 1, due to the very limited size of the output space (only 30 possible values in the test set)
supports: On an OMEGA probability task the base model reaches Pass@k = 1 at large k because the test answers take only 30 values.

quote: Maj@k is equivalent to Cover@τ with τ = 0.5.
supports: The paper equates majority-vote accuracy with Cover@0.5.

quote: However, when marginally increasing the threshold to τ = 0.025, the performance of the base model drops significantly
supports: On the OOD OMEGA split the base model's coverage falls sharply once τ is raised to 0.025.

quote: We train all models using the VERL framework (Sheng et al., 2024), starting from the Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct model
supports: All RLVR models in the paper start from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

quote: Our metric still accounts for the accuracy of the final answer, without evaluating the soundness of the reasoning trace
supports: The paper concedes Cover@τ grades final answers only and does not check reasoning soundness.

quote: base LLMs are capable of producing incorrect CoTs yet coincidentally arriving at the ground truth, especially for hard mathematical questions where answers are simple
supports: The paper says base-model Pass@K on maths is inflated by wrong chains that land on the right (guessable) answer.

quote: we introduce a new metric, CoT-Pass@K, which evaluates success only when both the final answer and the intermediate reasoning CoT are correct.
supports: CoT-Pass@K counts a sample only if both the answer and the chain of thought are judged correct.

quote: we verify the correctness of mathematical CoTs by instructing DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen38B (DeepSeek, 2025) and confirm their reliability.
supports: Chain correctness is judged by an LLM (DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B), not by hand.

quote: In our study, we employ n = 3 verification attempts for each CoT.
supports: Each chain is judged three times and aggregated by any-, all- or majority-correct rules.

quote: Here the base LLM is Qwen2.5-32B, and the post-RLVR model is DAPO-Qwen-32B.
supports: The maths comparison is a zero-RL pair: pretrained Qwen2.5-32B versus DAPO-Qwen-32B.

quote: the performance of the base LLM quickly catches up with and even surpasses the post-RLVR model as K increases.
supports: Under answer-only Pass@K the base model catches up with and passes the RL model at large K, as in Yue et al.

quote: reveal a consistent and significant performance gap between the models across all values of K (up to 1024).
supports: Under CoT-Pass@K on AIME 2024 and 2025 the RL model stays ahead of the base at every K up to 1,024.

quote: we manually inspect cases where the Pass@K metric yields a small positive value, but the CoT-Pass@K metric returns zero.
supports: The authors hand-inspect cases where answer-only Pass@K is positive but CoT-Pass@K is zero (examples in App. A.8).

quote: the effects of RLVR seem less pronounced, as the base LLM is already capable of solving these problems correctly with sufficient attempts
supports: On MATH-500 and AMC23 the base already solves the problems with enough attempts, so RLVR shows little boundary gain.

quote: code reasoning relies on the actual execution of generated code snippets to verify correctness, significantly reducing the likelihood of guessing.
supports: The paper treats code Pass@K as reliable because unit-test execution makes guessing unlikely.

quote: we can still observe a non-negligible portion of imperfect CoTs (the median of P (CC|CA)(q) is around 0.7).
supports: On fully optimised DAPO training questions the median share of correct-answer chains the judge accepts is about 0.7, so about 30 % are judged flawed.

quote: A key limitation of our study lies in the use of a LLM as the verifier for the correctness of reasoning CoTs
supports: The authors name the LLM judge (no large-scale hand check) as their key limitation.

quote: Here the distilled LLM is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and the post-RLVR model is AceReason-Nemotron-7B.
supports: The code comparison starts RL from a distilled long-CoT 7B model.

quote: Pass@k measures whether a model reaches a correct answer under repeated sampling, but never how: a lucky guess counts the same as sound reasoning.
supports: The audit frames Pass@k as blind to how an answer was reached.

quote: We observe that all three judges accept corrupted chains almost as often as clean ones.
supports: Under CoT-Pass@k's own protocol, three LLM judges accept injected-error chains nearly as often as clean ones.

quote: The metric’s own judge barely rejects even there, leaving 71% of the wrong answers accepted.
supports: CoT-Pass@k's specified judge (R1-distill) accepts 71 % of solutions whose final answer was corrupted.

quote: the difference Pass@k − CoT-Pass@k averages 19.7 points on an earlier solver generation but only 4.1 on the current one.
supports: The gap between Pass@k and CoT-Pass@k is 19.7 points for Qwen2.5 solvers but 4.1 for current solvers.

quote: raising the generation budget moves Pass@64 by more than fifty points while the difference stays at zero.
supports: Raising the token budget changes Pass@64 by over 50 points while the CoT filter removes nothing.

quote: Publish how the judge responds to injected errors.
supports: The audit recommends that any judged reasoning metric report its judge's response to injected errors.

quote: Sun et al. (2026) build valid-answer, invalid-reasoning solutions and find frontier judges credit up to half of them as flawless
supports: The audit reports concurrent work in which frontier judges pass up to half of right-answer, wrong-reasoning solutions.

quote: We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content.
supports: IFBench's verifier gives full credit to frontier-model responses that barely answer the request.

quote: in all three matched OLMo 3 (Olmo et al., 2025) DPO–RLVR pairs, the RLVR checkpoint achieves higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality
supports: In the OLMo 3 7B Instruct, 7B Think and 32B Think DPO-RLVR pairs, RLVR raises IFBench constraint satisfaction but lowers judged response quality.

quote: We compute the former as IFBench’s prompt-level loose accuracy and the latter as the mean 1–10 prompt–completion rating from strong LLM judges
supports: Constraint satisfaction is IFBench prompt-level loose accuracy; response quality is a 1-10 LLM-judge rating.

quote: returns only “No. 0 1 2 3 4,” under (x, c). Standard VIF evaluation counts this response as successful solely because it satisfies c
supports: The paper shows a constrained answer reduced to five numbers that IFBench still counts as a success.

quote: IF-RLVR achieves larger gains in Constraint Satisfaction (Figure 5), but its Fail → Pass outcomes show an average quality decline of 2.05 points.
supports: On prompts that the base fails and the IF-RLVR policy passes, judged quality falls by 2.05 points on average.

quote: This deterioration is not limited to Fail → Pass outcomes: Pass → Pass outcomes also show an average decline of 1.26 points.
supports: Quality also falls (1.26 points) on prompts both base and trained policy pass.

quote: This decline is accompanied by a marked reduction in response length, suggesting that the policy satisfies c while omitting substantive content needed to answer x.
supports: On the hardest (word-level) constraints IF-RLVR shortens responses while satisfying the constraint.

quote: IF-RLVR increases Constraint Satisfaction (0–100 scale) from 26.98 to 44.93 but reduces Response Quality (1–10 scale) from 4.51 to 2.96
supports: Averaged over the authors' five IF-RLVR runs, constraint satisfaction rises 26.98 to 44.93 and quality falls 4.51 to 2.96.

quote: To account for stochasticity, we repeat each evaluation three times and report the mean and standard deviation.
supports: Evaluations are repeated three times and averaged; no pass@k or reach analysis is reported.

quote: wires reveal that IntentCheck significantly reduces the reward hacking rate from 14.53% to 7.60%.
supports: IFDecorator's trap-instruction probes measure a reward-hacking rate that falls from 14.53 % to 7.60 % with IntentCheck.

quote: MHR measures the fraction of trip wire instructions where the current policy’s response exhibits at least one exploitative behavior pattern.
supports: The hack rate is the share of trap instructions whose response shows a predefined exploit pattern.

quote: Repetition: Satisfying requirements through trivial repetition, such as character/word count
supports: Trivial repetition to meet count constraints is one of four exploit patterns the paper lists.

quote: we define a baseline that enumerates answers according to their prevalence in the training set.
supports: The paper builds a guessing baseline that enumerates the most common training-set answers.

quote: this baseline outperforms repeated model sampling for some LLMs
supports: For some models the enumeration baseline beats repeated sampling in coverage.

quote: 97%, 91% and 73% for M ODEL A NSWERS, M IX TURE (M) with M = 10, and T RAIN C OUNTS respectively
supports: For Llama-3-70B on MATH at k = 1,000: model sampling 97 %, 10 samples plus enumeration 91 %, enumeration alone 73 %.

quote: “guessing” can become pronounced as k increases, where a model may generate an incorrect CoT but still accidentally arrive at the correct answer.
supports: Yue et al. name guessing at large k as a threat to maths pass@k.

quote: If a problem can be answered correctly with a low but non-zero probability (e.g., <5%), we consider it to be guessable and remove it.
supports: Yue et al. drop AIME24 problems that the base answers correctly without a chain of thought at a low rate (guessable).

quote: Applying it to AIME24 (30 questions) results in a subset of 18 questions.
supports: The guessability filter keeps 18 of 30 AIME24 problems.

quote: The base model answered 7 such questions, with 5 out of 6 containing at least one correct CoT
supports: A hand check of the base's correct answers on the hardest AIME24 problems (accuracy < 5 %) finds a correct chain on 5 of 6 (one ambiguous case excluded).

quote: Similarly, the RL-trained model answered 6 questions, 4 of which included at least one correct CoT.
supports: The same hand check finds a correct chain on 4 of the RL model's 6 hardest solved problems.

quote: We also see a decent improvement in pass@32 results, demonstrating that our run maintains diversity and RLVR pushes the model beyond its initial capabilities.
supports: Olmo 3 reads a pass@32 gain of RL-Zero (maths, AIME 2024/2025) as RLVR going beyond the base's capabilities.

quote: We show the main evaluation for the math domain: AIME 2024 and 2025 with pass@1, computed as a bootstrapped average over 32 samples, and pass@32.
supports: The RL-Zero evaluation uses AIME 2024 and 2025 with at most 32 samples.

location: §4.5 Key Findings (DPO remains a better starting point)
quote: prior work (Yue et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024) suggests RLVR, under certain conditions, helps convert pass@K improvements into pass@1 gains.
supports: Olmo 3 expects RLVR from the DPO Think model to turn pass@K into pass@1 gains.

location: §4.5 Key Findings (DPO remains a better starting point)
quote: we find that while the DPO model does display lower entropy, it in fact has higher pass@K performance on AIME evaluations
supports: The DPO Think model has higher AIME pass@K than the SFT model (K up to 32).

quote: we set k=16 to match the GRPO group size, which we observed to act as an empirical upper-bound on the possible improvement from RL training.
supports: Olmo 3 reports that base pass@16 acted as an empirical upper bound on RL improvement.

quote: raises Olmo-3-7B’s pass@1 accuracy from 42% to 78%, compared with 75% for its RL counterpart.
supports: Prefilling a two-token cue lifts the Olmo 3 7B base from 42 % to 78 % MATH-500 pass@1, against 75 % for RL-Zero.

quote: We use the released Olmo RL-Zero model and a Qwen3-14B model trained on MATH with GRPO and binary correctness rewards
supports: The RL counterpart for Olmo is the released Olmo RL-Zero model.

quote: The RL-Zero prompt is the one Ai2 used to train Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math
supports: The paper uses Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math and its training prompt.

quote: sampling 32 responses per problem with a 31,744-token budget unless noted
supports: Each problem gets 32 samples at a 31,744-token cap (pass@1, pass@16 reported).
Olmo-3-7B base on AIME 2024: pass@1 12.0 to 23.3 with the cue; pass@16 51.9 to 56.6.
Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math on AIME 2024 (RL-Zero prompt): pass@1 35.2, pass@16 68.6 without a cue.

quote: RL itself increases the probability of these cues, with policy changes concentrated at the first few output positions.
supports: The paper finds RL mostly raises the probability of the cue tokens at the first output positions.

quote: Math-Verify (Kydlíček, 2025) checks equivalence with the reference; extraction, parsing or verification failures count as incorrect.
supports: Grading is final-answer equivalence by Math-Verify; parse failures are scored wrong.

quote: Across nine public RLVR checkpoints at standard 3k–16k token limits, only one narrowly meets this criterion before multiplicity adjustment
supports: Of nine public RLVR pairs at 3k-16k tokens, only one meets a paired early-gain-plus-late-loss crossover test before multiplicity correction.

quote: per-response token limits alone can create, mask, or reverse a crossover through asymmetric truncation.
supports: Different truncation rates of base and RL model at a token cap can create, hide or reverse crossovers.

quote: truncated completions that fail to reach a boxed answer are scored as incorrect.
supports: Truncated generations count as failures, which penalises the model that truncates more.

quote: the R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B base model truncates 30.6% of its generations, compared with 12.2% for DeepScaleR and 2.0% for ProRL
supports: At 8k tokens the distilled base truncates far more often than its RL descendants.

quote: whereas two 7B long-chain RLVR models show no supported loss.
supports: On a clean 32k benchmark the two 7B RL models (from R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) show no statistically supported loss to their base.

quote: Skywork-OR1-7B (He et al., 2025) against their shared base R1-Distill-Qwen-7B
supports: The 7B pairs start RL from a distilled long-CoT model.

quote: a problem counts as expanded when the base model produced no correct sample in k draws and the trained model produces at least one.
supports: The paper names the usual expansion rule: base 0 of k, trained at least 1.

quote: a frozen Qwen3-8B evaluated twice at k=128 “expands” 7 of the 25 AIME problems it had not reached.
supports: A frozen model re-evaluated at k = 128 appears to expand 7 of 25 unreached AIME problems.

quote: All seven are single lucky samples
supports: All seven phantom expansions are single successes.

quote: over the 110 our experiments contain the null is 0.058 [0.038, 0.078], larger than the value it was supposed to certify.
supports: Even with a two-success threshold the measured null expansion rate is 0.058 across 110 frozen comparisons.

quote: F3 a fixed token cap under style drift: the most effective arm is scored the most destructive.
supports: A fixed token cap under a change of output style can invert which arm looks best.

quote: OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct (OLMo Team, 2025); 16 layers (d=2048); 13 checkpoints at steps 200–2600 (interval 200).
supports: The study uses 13 public OLMo 2 1B RLVR checkpoints (steps 200-2,600).

quote: pass@256 actually rises from 0.945 to 0.969 (Figure 1), so the set of problems the model can eventually solve grows, not shrinks.
supports: On GSM8K, pass@256 rises from 0.945 to 0.969 over the RLVR checkpoints.

quote: We evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across 16 checkpoints: SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final released RLVR checkpoint
supports: The paper evaluates Olmo 3 7B Think's public intermediate RLVR checkpoints (safety behaviour, not reach).

quote: we find that several widely cited gaps shrink substantially or disappear once budgets, prompts, and dataset versions are matched
supports: Budget- and prompt-matched reproductions shrink or remove several reported RLVR gaps.

quote: attempt inflation and calibration drift that convert abstentions into confident answers
supports: The paper names attempt inflation (abstentions turned into confident answers) as an RLVR confound.

quote: False positive rate is defined as the proportion of “false positives” among all responses deemed correct by the automatic evaluation.
supports: The paper measures the share of answer-correct responses whose reasoning is flawed (false positives).

quote: Human evaluation involves a meticulous, step-by-step review of the model’s responses by human annotators
supports: False positives are identified by step-by-step human review (the gold standard for its detection benchmark).

quote: the pass@N metric is more susceptible to “false positives” than other metrics in automatic evaluations
supports: The paper finds pass@N (any-of-N correct) admits more false positives than other inference-scaling metrics.

quote: False positive rates increase with benchmark difficulty.
supports: False-positive rates rise on harder benchmarks (AIME, Omni-MATH) for Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct.

quote: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Oat-Zero exhibits a higher false positive rate and demonstrates limited reflection and self-verification.
supports: A rule-based-reward GRPO model shows a higher false-positive rate than its instruct counterpart on AIME.

quote: due to resource constraints, we do not perform human detection on large-scale datasets.
supports: Human false-positive detection covers only part of the data.

quote: our analysis focuses on an R1-Zero-style setting (Guo et al., 2025) where RL is applied directly to a base model
supports: The authors restrict their cue-matches-RL claim to RL applied directly to a base model.

quote: Complex multi-stage post-training pipelines may introduce capabilities beyond those elicited by the token cues
supports: They leave open that multi-stage pipelines (SFT, DPO, then RL) add capabilities cues cannot elicit.

quote: from 0.14 to 0.65 in Olmo-3-7B
supports: In §2.3 (which sets up the authors' own 300-step GRPO runs from the base), RL raises the cue opening's probability in Olmo-3-7B from 0.14 to 0.65.

quote: Loglikelihood is computed under the corresponding DPO checkpoint, conditioned on the request alone.
supports: The likelihood in the OLMo 3 comparison is computed under each pair's DPO checkpoint, conditioned on the request without the constraint.

quote: compliance even as log-likelihood under x decreases. Indeed, OLMo 3 RLVR checkpoints exhibit this pattern, alongside a decline in Response Quality (Figure 3)
supports: The OLMo 3 RLVR checkpoints' IFBench responses have lower log-likelihood under the request alone than the DPO responses.

quote: Because pass@k estimates at adjacent k reuse the same generations and are nearly collinear, pointwise error bars cannot establish a sign change.
supports: The paper argues a visible crossover needs a paired test on the RL-minus-base difference curve, not pointwise error bars.

quote: all four GRPO arms fall behind the base near k ≈ 200 and remain behind through k = 4096
supports: In controlled runs (one 1.5B base, 3,000 new problems) the base overtakes every GRPO arm near k = 200 and stays ahead to k = 4,096.

quote: the unlocked prompts improve by a median factor of 2× to 7×
supports: Among prompts the base solves once in 128-256 attempts, the unlocked ones improve by a median factor of 2-7 after RL.

quote: over 99% of rollouts terminate naturally with a boxed answer, converging onto a single repeated wrong answer
supports: The RL losses (locked prompts) are not truncation or format failures but a repeated wrong answer.

quote: Report truncation rates and check token-limit sensitivity.
supports: The paper recommends reporting both models' truncation rates and testing token-limit sensitivity.

quote: our controlled GRPO and SFT runs use 100–132 updates on a 1.5B base model
supports: The controlled runs are short (100-132 updates) on a 1.5B base.

quote: for 30 epochs with a batch size of 500 and a mini-batch size of 96.
supports: OMEGA runs train for 30 epochs at batch size 500.

quote: Popular datasets for evaluating mathematical reasoning may suffer from data leakage
supports: The authors use procedurally generated OMEGA and Reasoning Gym tasks to limit contamination.

quote: This gap is particularly pronounced on AIME 2025, possibly due to its complete absence of unintentional data contamination
supports: The authors attribute the larger AIME 2025 gap to AIME 2025 postdating the base model training cutoff.

quote: we observe that AceReason-Nemotron-7B exhibits clear Pass@K improvements over DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on most benchmark versions
supports: On LiveCodeBench, RL from a distilled 7B start raises Pass@K up to K = 1,024.

quote: every solver draws 64 generations per question (16 on the Portuguese exams) at temperature 0.6
supports: The audit evaluates Pass@k and CoT-Pass@k at k up to 64.

quote: We use answer agreement as a proxy for accuracy without reference answers.
supports: The cue is chosen by a label-free answer-agreement (low answer entropy) criterion.

quote: this criterion selects a cue within 1.1 percentage points of the highest MATH-500 pass@1 among 500 tested openings
supports: On Olmo-3-7B the selected cue is within 1.1 points of the best of 500 openings on MATH-500.

quote: median visible length on the held-out validation prompts plummets from 114 to 28.5 words, and to 18 by step 390
supports: Training Qwen2.5-7B with GRPO on IFTrain rewards shrinks median validation responses from 114 to 18 words.

quote: IFTrain reaches 28.5% at step 180 and is still rising at 38% by step 390
supports: Fig. 9b: the share of validation completions scoring at least 0.8 with fewer than 30 words reaches 38 % by step 390 on IFTrain rewards.

quote: by step 180, bare constraint tokens with high rewards; by step 390 we see empty section headers, long repetitions of a single phrase
supports: Observed hacks include bare constraint tokens, empty section headers and repetition of a phrase.

quote: Anonymous authors (working draft; not submitted, not peer reviewed)
supports: The document is an anonymous, unsubmitted, non-peer-reviewed working draft.

quote: changes 2 strict verdicts but 257 of 348 loose verdicts
supports: A vacuous-truth defect in IFBench's format:sub-bullets checker flips 257 of 348 loose verdicts (pass to fail) but only 2 strict ones.

quote: a vacuous-truth defect lowers IFBench loose accuracy of a baseline from 20.3\% to 17.7\%
supports: Fixing the defect lowers a baseline's IFBench loose prompt accuracy from 20.3 % to 17.7 %.
